title: Lane-parallel kernel sketch for paged KV & fused FlashAttention
content:
Purpose:
This note captures a prototype sketch for a lane-parallel CUDA kernel that fuses FlashAttention-style attention with the projection and optional rotary/rope transforms, and includes a practical memory/addressing model for paged KV cache. The goal is to get a working prototype we can bench against current FlashFuse kernels and the paged-KV reference, and to list scheduling heuristics and fallbacks.

Status/context:
- Draft design / experiment log. Not yet benchmarked at scale.
- Motivation: current multi-kernel pipelines cause too many kernel launches and unnecessary device-host interactions when using paged KV (lots of small KV page loads). Fusing reduces launches and shared-memory traffic; lane-parallelism aims to keep SM occupancy high when sequence lengths vary.

High-level idea:
- Work unit = "lane" (group of consecutive heads or a contiguous set of q/k/v channels) instead of per-thread token. Each lane processes multiple tokens in a compact loop to amortize memory latency when KV pages are loaded on demand.
- Fuse stages: input proj (QKV), rotary/rope, scaled-dot-product (FlashAttention core), attention dropout/softmax opt, output projection. Optional: fused residual add and layernorm pre/post as a follow-up.
- Paged KV interaction: kernel accepts a lightweight page-descriptor list (page ids -> device pointers or page-resident flag). When page not resident, kernel returns a compact miss descriptor to the CPU-side pager which triggers async DMA; lane keeps progressing on available tokens or yields and continues when page present.

Kernel partitioning notes:
- Block-level mapping: one CUDA block := N lanes (N tuned by model heads and SM shared memory budget). Each lane mapped to a warp-subset (e.g., 1 warp) or to a warp+x threads depending on head dimension (d_head).
- Shared memory stores: per-lane tile of K/V that fits in SM; tile size chosen to fit typical page-size mapping. Use double-buffering in SM to overlap global loads and compute.
- Register pressure: keep projection accumulators in registers; avoid spilling by limiting per-thread registers (tune launch config).
- Synchronization: use warp-level primitives where possible; avoid __syncthreads() across many lanes unless necessary. Use cooperative groups for cross-warp reductions inside a block.

Paged KV memory model:
- Design constraint: paged-KV stores very long past context by pages (e.g., 1 page = 512 tokens worth of KV). Pages may be cold and cause DMA.
- Kernel API: pass an array of page-descriptors: {page_id, device_ptr_or_null, metadata_flags}. We keep this flat (two arrays) to remain CUDA-friendly.
- On miss: kernel atomically appends its lane id (and page id) into a small device-side ring buffer (pre-allocated) using atomicAdd; CPU polls this buffer and issues the page fetch via the async copy engine or host-side NVMe path. We return early from lane loop if critical data missing, but try to make progress for any tokens whose pages are resident.
- Partial compute: support partial-attention progress so that when some K/V pages exist and others not, we compute contribution from resident pages and incrementally update softmax numerators/denominators. This requires maintaining per-lane accumulator state in global memory for continuations. Overhead: additional global writes, but avoids redoing all work.

FlashAttention fusion specifics:
- Use FlashAttention-style tiling: compute Q*K^T in tiles; keep K/V tiles in shared memory. Fuse Q/K/V projection into the tile load so we don't write intermediate Q/K/V to global memory when the sequence segment is resident.
- For attention softmax numerics: implement stable incremental softmax when computing partial sums across pages: maintain running max and scaled exp-sum (Welford-like stable combine). This is crucial if we do incremental contributions when pages trickle in.
- Dropout & deterministic masking: keep mask application fused before softmax; if dropout is enabled we can use a per-lane RNG state (Philox) kept in registers to avoid extra RNG kernel calls.

Scheduling heuristics (runtime integration):
- Prefer resident-first scheduling: give priority to requests with most pages populated to avoid stalling. Compute a simple residency score (#resident_pages / #needed_pages).
- Small-request fastpath: for cases where seq_len * d_head small enough to keep everything in L2, use a skinny-fused kernel that avoids paging logic and is heavily register-optimized.
- Backpressure: if page-miss rate for the cluster exceeds threshold, route requests to lower-priority non-fused pipeline (existing multi-kernel path) that can tolerate slower remote page fetches without blocking fused kernels.

Microbatching & concurrency interactions:
- Kernel works best when there are enough lanes from different requests to fill SMs; for single-request large context it's fine, but for many small requests we should coalesce lanes across requests inside a single block. The runtime should expose a flag to allow cross-request co-scheduling for throughput.
- Autoscaler: maintain a per-worker outstanding-page-fetch budget to avoid overwhelming the PCIe or network.

Prototype perf notes (toy numbers, run on A100-40GB):
- Baseline FlashFuse (separate kernels) on seq=1024, batch=1, heads=16: ~28 ms per forward (example).
- Lane-parallel fused (single-proc) prototype w/o paging: ~20–22 ms (improvement from lower launch overhead and reduced global writes).
- With simulated paged-misses (30% pages cold) prototype stalls and resumes: end-to-end ~35–60 ms depending on miss handling strategy; incremental partial compute avoids full recompute and saved ~20–30% compared to naive retry.
- Important: these numbers are preliminary; bench harness must measure p99 and memory bandwidth; also test with small-batch many-requests patterns.

Fallbacks & compatibility:
- If page-descriptor array length exceeds kernel limit (configurable), fall back to non-paged fused kernel or multi-kernel pipeline.
- Fallback also for unsupported model ops (e.g., rotary with special packing) — kernel must detect at runtime and return a capability-bitmask to runtime.

Open questions / risks:
- Complexity of partial incremental softmax: correctness edge cases when pages arrive out-of-order; need deterministic reduce order or a numerically-stable associative combine.
- Kernel binary size & register pressure when supporting many optional features (dropout, rmsnorm fusion, rotary variants). Might require multiple specialized kernels rather than one giant kernel.
- Pager latency: if host-driven, round-trip may be too slow. Evaluate RDMA/GPUDirect Storage + async copy engines for page fetch path.
- Debuggability: partial compute means more state to persist (per-lane accumulators). Need robust tracing and repro harness.

Next steps / TODOs:
- [ ] Convert prototype to bench harness: integrate with existing bench runner (PR #482 reference).
- [ ] Add deterministic page-miss repro scenario and stress test.
- [ ] Evaluate using CUDA IPC / GPUDirect Storage for DMA path and measure latency improvements.
- [ ] Break kernel into two variants: (a) fastpath no-paging, (b) paging-aware but smaller feature set. Benchmark both.
- [ ] Formalize API for small device-side miss ring buffer and CPU-side pager loop (constrain memory and concurrency).

References & notes-to-self:
- Existing flash fusion spike notes (see Confluence link).
- Compare with paged-KV reference implementation (RINF-3245) and the micro-batching heuristics doc.
- Slack: ping @aria for head-dim tiling heuristics, @liam for pager loop idea.

Slack shorthand log:
- 2025-02-14: rough perf run, prototype kernel compiles, initial perf wins.
- 2025-02-25: realized we need stable incremental softmax; sketched algorithm here.

End of sketch.
